title: Prompt Design
scopeHtml: Scope: System prompts, few-shot, chain of thought, delimiters and iteration.

notes.title: System prompts and roles
notes.html:
What a system prompt is. A message with elevated authority at the start of the conversation that defines the assistant's standing behaviour. Providers expose it as a separate field (system) or a system/developer role message. It persists for the whole conversation, while user turns carry the individual tasks. Models are trained to weigh system instructions above user instructions when they conflict, although this hierarchy is not an absolute security boundary.

What belongs in it.

  1. Role and audience: "You are a support assistant for Acme's billing product, talking to non-technical customers."
  2. Scope: what to help with and what to decline or redirect.
  3. Style and tone: formal/friendly, length limits, language, formatting.
  4. Output format: JSON schema, sections, citation style.
  5. Rules and policies: never reveal internal notes, never give legal advice, escalate when X.
  6. Behaviour under uncertainty: ask a clarifying question, say "I don't know", return null.
  7. Tool-use guidance: when to call which tool.
  8. Stable reference material (policies, glossaries) when appropriate (and cacheable).

What does not belong. Per-request data (put it in the user turn or a dedicated block), secrets (assume the model may reveal system prompts), and vague aspirations ("be great").

Design principles.

  • Specific and testable: every sentence should correspond to a behaviour you can check in an eval.
  • Positive and negative: say what to do, and for important boundaries also what not to do, with the reason.
  • Priority order: when rules conflict, say which wins.
  • Explain the why: models follow instructions better when they understand the goal ("Keep answers under 80 words because they are shown on a smartwatch").
  • Place stable text first so prefix caching works; put volatile data later.
  • Version it (see lifecycle notes).

Failure modes. Drift over long conversations (rules forgotten as context grows) → restate critical rules near the end, keep the system prompt short and prioritized; conflicting instructions → resolve explicitly; over-long prompts → dilution (each added rule weakens the others).

Real life. A job description and company handbook (system prompt) versus today's task list (user message).

Interview angle. What goes in the system prompt vs user turn; why it is not a security boundary; how to keep it from bloating.

notes.title: Few-shot examples
notes.html:
What they do. Show 1 to 8 input→output examples inside the prompt. They teach pattern: exact format, tone, labels, edge-case handling. They don't teach facts and are not training (no weights change), but models imitate them strongly ("in-context learning").

How to choose examples.

  • Representative: cover the main input types.
  • Diverse: different lengths, phrasings, labels.
  • Correct: errors in examples are copied. Take them from high-scoring real outputs or have an expert verify.
  • Include edge cases: ambiguous inputs, empty fields, "not applicable", refusals.
  • Balanced labels: if 4 of 5 examples are "positive", the model skews positive.
  • Order matters: recency bias means the last example can influence the output; shuffle and test.
  • Consistent format: same delimiters and tags in every example.

Cost. Examples use tokens on every call. Start with zero-shot; add one; add more only if the eval improves. For large example sets use dynamic few-shot: retrieve the most similar examples for each query from a library (kNN selection) to improve relevance with fewer tokens.

Zero-, one- and few-shot. Zero-shot: instructions only. One-shot: one example. Few-shot: several. Capable models often do well zero-shot, but a couple of examples still help with strict formats and subtle labelling conventions.

Format example.

<example>
  <input>I was charged twice this month.</input>
  <output>BILLING</output>
</example>
<example>
  <input>The app crashes when I upload a photo.</input>
  <output>TECHNICAL</output>
</example>

Pitfalls. Over-fitting to examples (model copies phrasing or content), leakage of example content into answers, examples contradicting the instructions, and tag formats that are also used in the user data.

Real life. Handing a new hire a few finished reports instead of describing the format in words.

notes.title: Chain of thought and reasoning
notes.html:
Chain-of-thought (CoT). Asking the model to reason step by step before answering ("Think step by step", or examples that include reasoning) improves performance on arithmetic, logic, multi-hop questions, planning and code reasoning. Mechanism: generating intermediate tokens gives the model more computation per answer and a scratchpad to store partial results (a fixed-depth network can only do so much computation in one forward pass).

Variants.

  • Zero-shot CoT: just add "Let's think step by step".
  • Few-shot CoT: examples with reasoning.
  • Self-consistency: sample several reasoning paths and take the majority answer.
  • Decomposition / least-to-most: break the problem into subquestions solved in order.
  • Plan then solve, verify then answer, scratchpad in tags (<thinking>/<answer>).
  • Reasoning models perform this internally; they need goals and constraints more than step-by-step scripts.

When it helps / hurts. Helps multi-step problems. Adds cost and latency and gives no gain on lookups, classification and simple extraction. Can hurt on tasks where "overthinking" produces wrong justifications, and can leak reasoning you don't want shown.

Practical patterns. Put reasoning in a separate field or tags and parse only the final answer; with structured output put a reasoning field before the answer field so the model reasons first. Don't treat displayed reasoning as a faithful explanation of the model's internal computation; it can be post-hoc.

Real life. Showing your working in maths: it catches errors, but is wasted on 2 + 2.

notes.title: Delimiters and structure
notes.html:
Why. Prompts mix instructions, context documents, examples, and user input. Without clear boundaries, the model may treat data as instructions or mix up sections. Delimiters reduce ambiguity and make it harder (not impossible) for injected text to masquerade as instructions.

Practices.

  • Use XML-style tags with descriptive names (<document>, <user_question>, <rules>); headings and triple-quoted blocks also work.
  • Wrap each long document with an index and source: <doc id="3" source="policy.pdf">...</doc>; ask the model to cite ids.
  • Put long reference material before the question; end with the task restated.
  • Be consistent: same tag names everywhere, referenced in instructions ("Answer using only the content in <documents>").
  • Escape or strip tag-like sequences in untrusted text so it cannot close your tags.
  • Keep structure shallow; nested complexity confuses smaller models.

Real life. Labelled folders in a filing cabinet instead of one pile of paper.

notes.title: Common prompt patterns
notes.html:
Pattern Use Key ingredients
Task + format + constraints most tasks what, shape, limits, audience
Persona/role tone and domain framing specific role, not "expert" fluff
Extraction structured data from text schema, "null if absent", quote evidence
Classification routing, tagging closed label set, definitions, examples, "other"
Transformation/rewrite edit, translate, summarize what must not change, length, style
Q&A over context RAG answer only from context, cite, say unknown
Self-check / critique quality rubric, then revise
Decomposition / chaining complex workflows small prompts, validated hand-offs
Role-play / simulation testing, training clear boundaries
Meta-prompting generate prompts use sparingly; evaluate output

Prompt chaining vs one big prompt. Chains (extract → validate → generate) are easier to test and debug, allow different models per step, and let you branch; they cost more calls and latency. Use when a single prompt is unreliable or when intermediate outputs need validation.

Real life. A toolbox: pick the pattern that fits the job.

notes.title: The iteration loop
notes.html:
1. Define success with examples and a metric (what does a good answer look like?).
  2. Build a small eval set (20 to 100 realistic and edge-case inputs).
  3. Baseline with the simplest prompt.
  4. Diagnose the failures by type: wrong format, missing info, hallucination, scope drift, edge-case failure, tone.
  5. Change one thing targeting the dominant failure (add an output constraint, an example, a rule, a delimiter).
  6. Re-run the eval; keep the change only if it helps without regressions.
  7. Stop when the metric meets the bar; resist endless polishing.

Anti-patterns. Adding more words when the real problem is a missing structural piece; testing on three hand-picked examples; changing several things at once; tuning to the eval set until it overfits; prompts that keep growing; ignoring variance (run multiple samples).

Diagnosis table. Wrong shape → output constraint/schema. Drift across turns → sharper system prompt. Invented structure → examples. Breaks on rare variants → add the variant to constraints/examples. Hallucinated facts → grounding/retrieval. Too verbose → length limit + example.

Real life. Tuning a recipe: change one ingredient per attempt, taste, note the result.

notes.title: Prompting for different model types
notes.html:
Reasoning models. Give the goal, constraints, and success criteria; avoid prescribing detailed step-by-step procedures or "think step by step" (they already do); keep prompts concise; use effort/budget settings; expect longer latency.

Large non-reasoning models. Respond well to clear instructions and light structure; CoT helps on hard problems.

Small models. Need more explicit structure, shorter prompts, strong examples, simpler tasks per call, and stricter output constraints; test more.

Fine-tuned models. May need a different (shorter) prompt than the base; prompts used in training should match inference.

Multilingual and multimodal. State the output language explicitly; for images describe what to look for and how to handle ambiguity; test each language.

Portability. A prompt tuned for one model is not guaranteed to transfer; keep an eval suite and re-tune per model; avoid relying on quirks.

Real life. Briefing a senior engineer (goals and constraints) versus an intern (detailed steps and examples).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
System prompt. Standing contract: role, scope, tone, format, rules, behaviour under uncertainty. Specific, testable, prioritized, versioned, with stable content first for caching; keep it short to avoid dilution; it is not a security boundary.

Few-shot. Examples teach pattern, not facts. Choose representative, diverse, correct examples including edge cases; mind label balance and order; consider dynamic selection; each example costs tokens on every call.

Reasoning. Chain-of-thought helps multi-step tasks, hurts cost/latency on simple ones; use self-consistency, decomposition, scratchpad tags, reasoning-before-answer fields; reasoning models need goals not scripts; displayed reasoning is not guaranteed faithful.

Structure. Delimit data from instructions with descriptive tags; index and cite documents; put long context first and the task last; escape untrusted tags.

Patterns. Task+format+constraints, extraction, classification, Q&A over context, transformation, self-check, chaining.

Iteration. Eval set first; diagnose failure type; change one thing; measure; stop when good enough.

Model differences. Tune and test prompts per model type; do not assume portability.

Interview one-liners.

  • "Diagnose the failure, then add the missing structural piece, instead of adding words."
  • "Few-shot teaches format and edge cases; it costs tokens every call."
  • "Delimiters reduce confusion and injection risk but are a soft boundary."
  • "Reasoning models want goals and constraints, not step-by-step scripts."
